facts.statehood_note: Admitted the same day as North Dakota. President Benjamin Harrison shuffled the two proclamations so no one would know which he signed first; South Dakota is listed as the 40th state.

symbols.name: American pasque flower (adopted 1903; its motto is "I lead")

facts.name_origin: Named for the Dakota people (part of the Oceti Sakowin, or Seven Council Fires); "dakota" is a Sioux word meaning "friend" or "ally." The state was once the southern part of Dakota Territory.

government.chambers: Senate (35) and House of Representatives (70); each of the 35 legislative districts elects one senator and two representatives
government.executive: Governor (4-year term, limit of two terms in a row), leads the departments that run state government; the lieutenant governor runs on the same team and presides over the Senate
government.courts: South Dakota Supreme Court (5 justices, one from each of five districts; they choose their own chief justice). Seven judicial circuits hold the main trial courts, and magistrate courts serve every circuit.
government.local: 66 counties, plus cities and towns; nine tribal nations govern their own reservations
government.constitution: Current constitution adopted in 1889, written at a third constitutional convention after earlier ones in 1883 and 1885
government.kid_line: "it shall be the duty of the Legislature to establish and maintain a general and uniform system of public schools wherein tuition shall be without charge, and equally open to all" (Article VIII, Section 1)

long_ago.nation: Village farmers at the Mitchell site
long_ago.about: About 1,000 years ago, people built a village on a bluff above a creek near present-day Mitchell, protected by a ditch and a wall of log posts. They farmed the rich soil, fished, and hunted the nearby buffalo herds.

The Arikara lived in fortified earthlodge villages along the Missouri River. In 1804 Lewis and Clark met them in three villages at the mouth of the Grand River in northern South Dakota and estimated about 3,000 people.

The Lakota, the largest group of the Oceti Sakowin (Seven Council Fires), have seven bands, including the Oglala, Hunkpapa, and Sicangu. They moved across their lands as needs arose, hunted and gathered only what they needed, and wasted nothing.

The Dakota and Nakota speak the other two dialects of the Oceti Sakowin language. Their bands, such as the Sisseton, Wahpeton, and Ihanktonwan (Yankton), lived mainly in South Dakota and neighboring states such as Minnesota, Nebraska, and Montana.
The Cheyenne, like the Lakota, hold Bear Butte sacred; they call it Noahvose. People still come there to pray and leave prayer cloths and tobacco ties in the trees.

today.about: Lakota bands (Minnecoujou, Two Kettle, Sans Arc, and Blackfoot) on the Cheyenne River Reservation, with headquarters at Eagle Butte.
Lakota nation of the Pine Ridge Reservation, headquartered at Pine Ridge and led by an 18-member tribal council.
Sicangu (Brule) Lakota nation of the Rosebud Reservation, headquartered at Rosebud.
Its reservation crosses the North Dakota and South Dakota line; headquarters are at Fort Yates, North Dakota.
Dakota nation of the former Lake Traverse Reservation in northeastern South Dakota, headquartered at Agency Village.
Nakota nation of the Yankton Reservation in Charles Mix County, headquartered at Wagner.
Nation of the Crow Creek Reservation along the Missouri River, headquartered at Fort Thompson.
Nation of the Lower Brule Reservation; its tribal farm is described by the state as the nation's top popcorn producer.

first_peoples.today_note: The South Dakota Department of Tribal Relations works with nine tribal nations: the eight above plus the Flandreau Santee Sioux Tribe in Moody County. The Arikara now live mainly with the Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara Nation in North Dakota. Ownership of the Black Hills is still in legal dispute between the Sioux Nation and the U.S. government.
sites: Mitchell Prehistoric Indian Village (a village site about 1,000 years old where visitors can watch archaeologists work)
Bear Butte State Park (Mato Paha, "Bear Mountain," sacred to the Lakota, Cheyenne, and other nations)
Wind Cave National Park (tied to the Lakota emergence story)
The Black Hills (Paha Sapa), promised to the Sioux in the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty

history.event: Farming people build a protected village above a creek near present-day Mitchell.
The La Verendrye brothers, French explorers, bury a lead plate near present-day Fort Pierre to claim the land for France.
The Lakota and other Oceti Sakowin nations become the strongest power on the northern Plains.
The United States buys the Louisiana Territory from France, which includes present-day South Dakota.
Lewis and Clark meet the Arikara in three villages at the mouth of the Grand River.
An American fur trading post is set up at present-day Fort Pierre, the first lasting American settlement.
Smallpox devastates the Arikara, who had moved north to live near the Mandan.
The Yankton Sioux sign a treaty giving up most of eastern South Dakota.
During the Civil War, the First Dakota Cavalry serves on the Union side inside Dakota Territory.
On April 29, the Fort Laramie Treaty recognizes the Black Hills as part of the Great Sioux Reservation, set aside for the Sioux people.
George A. Custer leads an army expedition with gold seekers into the Black Hills. Gold is found, and miners pour onto Sioux land.
The U.S. government takes the Black Hills, breaking the promise of the 1868 treaty.
South Dakota becomes a state on November 2, the same day as North Dakota.

trailblazers.name: Sitting Bull (Tatanka-Iyotanka)
trailblazers.text: Born near where the Grand and Missouri Rivers meet in present-day South Dakota, Sitting Bull was a hunter, warrior, and spiritual leader. He refused the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty and led Lakota people who would not live on a reservation. He was shot when Lakota police came to arrest him at his cabin on December 15, 1890.

trailblazers.name: Fee Lee Wong (Wing Tsue)
trailblazers.text: Fee Lee Wong came to Deadwood in December 1876 and stayed 43 years. His Wing Tsue Bazaar anchored Deadwood's Chinatown, and he invited townspeople to Chinese New Year celebrations. In 1902 the Chinese Exclusion Act nearly kept him from coming home after a trip to China, until local leaders spoke up for him.

trailblazers.name: Zitkala-Sa (Gertrude Simmons Bonnin)
trailblazers.group: Yankton Dakota woman, writer and activist
trailblazers.text: Born on the Yankton Reservation, Zitkala-Sa wrote stories that challenged stereotypes and criticized boarding schools. She helped write The Sun Dance Opera (1913), called the first American Indian opera. In 1926 she co-founded the National Council of American Indians, a group that worked for Native voting rights.

trailblazers.name: Oscar Micheaux
trailblazers.group: Black American homesteader, author, and filmmaker
trailblazers.text: The son of formerly enslaved parents, Micheaux bought a homestead claim in Gregory County in 1905. He wrote novels about pioneer life, including The Conquest (1912). His film The Homesteader is called the first feature-length film by an African American, and he made 43 movies showing Black life without stereotypes.

trailblazers.name: Gladys Pyle
trailblazers.text: From Huron, Gladys Pyle was the first woman elected to the South Dakota legislature and the first woman elected South Dakota Secretary of State. In 1938 she became the first Republican woman elected to the U.S. Senate, and the first woman of any party elected to the Senate without first being appointed.

trailblazers.name: Billy Mills
trailblazers.text: Born in Pine Ridge, Billy Mills won the 10,000-meter race at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics in a famous upset. He is the first American to win Olympic gold in that race. In 1986 he co-founded Running Strong for American Indian Youth.

landforms: Black Hills (pine-covered low mountains in the southwest)
Black Elk Peak (formerly Harney Peak), highest point at 7,242 feet
Coteau des Prairies (a plateau in the east)
waters: Lake Oahe, Lake Sharpe, Lake Francis Case, and Lewis and Clark Lake (reservoirs behind Missouri River dams)
James, Big Sioux, Cheyenne, and White Rivers
Glacial lakes of eastern South Dakota
geography.regions: The Missouri River splits the state into East River (glacial lakes and farm prairie) and West River (Great Plains, Badlands, and the Black Hills).

ecosystems.name: Mixed-grass prairie
ecosystems.about: Badlands National Park protects mixed-grass prairie where bison, bighorn sheep, prairie dogs, and endangered black-footed ferrets live.

ecosystems.name: Badlands fossil beds
ecosystems.about: The Badlands hold one of the world's richest fossil beds, with remains of ancient horses and rhinos.

ecosystems.name: Caves under the Black Hills
ecosystems.about: Wind Cave is famous for boxwork, a rare honeycomb-shaped rock that hangs from ceilings and walls. Above it, a bison herd brought from the Bronx Zoo in 1913 roams the prairie.

ecosystems.name: Black Hills forest
ecosystems.about: The Black Hills are low mountains covered in pine forest; the Black Hills spruce is the state tree.

science.weather: Continental climate with four strong seasons: hot summers, very cold winters, blizzards and ice storms. About 30 tornadoes a year, and eastern South Dakota is often counted in Tornado Alley. Record high 120 F (Usta, 2006); record low -58 F (McIntosh, 1936).
science.resources: Farming and ranching (cattle, corn, soybeans, wheat, hogs), ethanol, tourism in the Black Hills, and services such as banking and health care.
science.highlight: The Mammoth Site in Hot Springs: a sinkhole filled with warm water trapped mammoths that could not climb out. Since 1974, 61 skeletons have been found (58 Columbian and 3 woolly mammoths), and new research dates the sinkhole to 160,000 to 232,000 years old.
